newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's embattled Fujimori cuts tax, ups salaries.
newsitem.headline: Peru's embattled Fujimori cuts tax, ups salaries.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori tried on Monday to defuse a political crisis by offering lower taxes and higher salaries to an increasingly hostile public.

In his annual State of the Nation address to Congress, the president, whose popularity has plummeted in recent months to record lows in the opinion polls, announced a 15 percent pay increase for public-sector employees and a reduction in a general housing tax.

Fujimori also assured his electorate he recognised as "completely understandable" public demands for more jobs and less poverty. "All our policies have one common denominator -- to create employment and reduce poverty," he said.

But despite the departure of ministers from his cabinet, a slew of scandals over alleged alleged abuses of power and the largest street protests in his seven years in office, Fujimori played down current political turmoil.

"The actual circumstances seem to be producing an obvious contradiction: a solid, growing economy ... going hand in hand with a confused political situation," he said. "This is a contradiction that I am sure all Peruvians want to overcome."
The president reminded Peru's public of his economic achievements: slashing the country's foreign debt, boosting international reserve levels and bringing runaway inflation under control.

But opposition congressmen lambasted Fujimori for offering no tangible measures to end the instability, which has weakened the president so dramatically some commentators say they fear the military could respond with a coup.

"(The speech) was the same as always," Jorge Avendano, a legislator with the opposition Union for Peru, said. "Always the great economic successes without saying anything to solve the political problem."

The opposition had specifically called on Fujimori to use his speech to announce the dismissal of military chief Nicolas de Bari Hermoza Rios and of the head of the national intelligence service, Vladimiro Montesinos, thought by most Peruvians to be the real power-holders in Peru.
Fujimori tried to calm public concern that the security forces dictate his policies, a widespread perception that has damaged his popularity.
"The armed forces have kept to their role according to the constitution," Fujimori said. "Their subordination to the president is an undoubtable fact."

Shortly before Fujimori's address, de Bari gave the president a vote of confidence, saying, "The president is the guarantee that our country has become stable ... that there is a scenario of security for international investors."
The president also countered claims the security forces repressed the media, saying Peru "exercises complete press freedom," because "criticism benefits the country."
But Fujimori's speech ignored the key issue of his possible candidacy in the 2000 presidential elections.
The opposition had called on him to make clear he would not seek an unprecedented third term in office, and most Peruvians want a referendum to decide if he can.
The public is divided over whether Fujimori is eligible to run for office again because of ambiguities in the constitution.

But manoeuvres by his supporters to remove obstacles to his candidacy -- including the ouster of three independent Constitutional Court judges in May -- angered Peruvians and precipitated the president's fall in the polls.
Fujimori, who has not said if he hopes to run in 2000, said late on Sunday he wanted to "leave the country solid, strong, viable and with enormous possibilities for everyone in the year 2000."
